column3: It closely parallels Pharaoh's circle calling Moses a corrupter and answering with a plan to kill the believing community's sons.

The council's claim that Moses wants to expel the people from their land supplies the same ruling-class alarm used to justify coercion.
Pharaoh treats the magicians' belief as an unauthorized plot to expel him, revealing how faith in Moses is recast as political subversion.
Pharaoh threatens the believing magicians with mutilation and crucifixion after they accept Moses, showing the coercive enforcement behind his religious claim.
The same threat against the magicians directly shows Pharaoh punishing adherence to Moses as a challenge to his authority.
A man warns Moses that the chiefs are taking counsel to kill him, supplying the immediate narrative reality of the threat voiced in the focus.
Pharaoh's people accuse Moses and Aaron of turning them from ancestral religion to gain supremacy, closely matching the focus's fear of religious change.
The immediately preceding identification of Moses as a magician and liar records the slander that prepares Pharaoh's call for violence.
Pharaoh's public claim of dominion over Egypt displays the political sovereignty that he seeks to preserve by discrediting Moses.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord exposes the ultimate authority claim beneath his opposition to Moses' Lord.
The sending of Moses with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs establishes the confrontation that later becomes an accusation of corruption.
Pharaoh's chiefs label Moses a learned magician, supplying the earlier delegitimizing charge behind their alarm.
Pharaoh's threat to cut off hands and feet and crucify the magicians shows his regime enforcing loyalty through exemplary violence.
Moses and Aaron are sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who respond with arrogant rejection.
The command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed gives God's contrary assessment of the ruler calling Moses corrupting.
Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh specifically because of his transgression, framing the focus's charge as reversal.
Pharaoh gathers his stratagem and appointed assembly against Moses, showing his opposition organized as public power.
The magicians' sudden belief in the Lord of Moses and Aaron explains the rupture that provokes Pharaoh's subsequent threat.
Pharaoh presents Moses to his chiefs as a learned magician, continuing the campaign to define the messenger as a public danger.
The chiefs repeat that Moses seeks to expel them from their land, a close political counterpart to the focus's allegation.
When Moses brings clear signs, Pharaoh's circle calls them fabricated magic and denies precedent, supplying the rejection that precedes the threat.
The surah's account of Moses' mission with authority and clear proof begins the immediate narrative unit containing the focus.

Pharaoh's order to build a tower so he can look upon Moses' God develops his attempt to replace response to signs with sovereign spectacle.

His demand for material tokens of rank continues the public effort to disqualify Moses rather than answer his message.
Pharaoh manipulates his people into obedience, showing how his accusation against Moses functions through a compliant public.

Moses' demand that they yield to God's servants directly conflicts with Pharaoh's claim to command the religious-political order.
Moses seeks refuge from their intended stoning, adding a direct threat of violence to the Pharaoh confrontation.

Pharaoh calls Moses bewitched despite the clear signs, furnishing another instance of his counter-accusation against the messenger.
